system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2190-10-10 10:52:00 to 2190-10-12 16:49:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

this admission, since it would probably mean that the patient 
would have to be on dialysis afterwards.  The plan is to have 
the patient follow up with Dr. ___ as an outpatient to further 
discuss further management.  She was discharged on increased 
doses of carvedilol and amlodipine, along with a prescription 
for sublingual nitroglycerin to be used if she has chest pain.  
Patient has follow up scheduled with Dr. ___ 
cardiologist, and her PCP/nephrologist after discharge.
  
# Mitral regurgitation: moderate to severe on last transthoracic 
echocardiogram, but was likely underestimated.  Catheterization 
was to be performed as part of evaluation for mitral valve 
replacement.  Patient reported, on admission, of being 
symptomatic with dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, and peripheral 
edema while at home.  She was also found to have an elevated 
JVP.  Patient was hypertensive during her first day of admission 
and carvedilol dose was increased as well as her amlodipine.  
Her home dose of lisinopril was discontinued due to acute kidney 
injury.  Patient will follow up with Dr. ___ to further 
discuss mitral valve repair in the future.

# Acute on chronic kidney disease s/p kidney transplant: patient 
is on tacrolimus, sirolimus and prednisone, and is chronic 
kidney disease stage V status post deceased donor renal 
transplant in ___ with subsequent allograft failure.  She is 
currently awaiting living donor transplant, and was reluctant to 
undergo dialysis.  Baseline creatinine was reportedly 2.6-3.2 
prior to admission, with admission creatinine being 3.9, 
representing acute kidney injury.  Cardiac catheterization was 
postponed due to high risk of renal failure and permanent 
hemodialysis.  Patient was continued on her home dose of 
tacrolimus, sirolimus and prednisone and daily tacrolimus levels 
were checked.  Renal transplant ultrasound was performed and 
showed no acute abnormality.  Urine electrolytes showed FEUrea 
of 40, representing interstitial injury.  Nephrotoxins were 
avoided, lisinopril was discontinued, and medications were 
renally dosed.  She was continued on calcium and Vitamin D 
supplementation.  Nephrology was consulted and patient stated 
that she refuses dialysis at the current time.  She will follow 
up with her PCP, who is also a nephrologist, for further 
management.

# Hypertension: patient was hypertensive soon after admission.  
Her carvedilol and amlodipine dose was increased due to 
hypertension during her hospital course.  Her lisinopril was 
stopped due to her worsened renal function noted below.  Patient 
was continued on her home hydralazine.  She will resume 
increased doses of carvedilol and amlodipine, as well as his 
home dose of hydralazine.

INACTIVE ISSUES
---------------  
# Rhythm analysis: patient was monitored on telemetry, and 
patient remained in normal sinus rhythm during her admission.
  
# Diabetes mellitus type 1: patient is status post pancreas and 
kidney transplant, and has not been on any therapy.  She was 
continued on her home dose of tacrolimus, sirolimus and 
prednisone, and daily tacrolimus levels were trended. 

# Hyperlipidemia: patient was continued on her home dose of 
rosuvastatin, which she should continue as an outpatient, goal 
LDL<70.

# Anemia: etiology likely secondary to kidney disease.  Patient 
did not require transfusion during hospitalization, and her 
hematocrit remained stable during hospitalization.
  
TRANSITION OF CARE
------------------

radiology_notes.text:
PORTABLE CHEST, ___

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS:  Heart size remains normal.  Lungs are clear except for a small
linear area of atelectasis in the right mid lung.  No pleural effusion.

IMPRESSION:  No evidence of pulmonary edema.

INDICATION:  A ___ female with acute kidney insufficiency, elective
cardiac catheterization, status post renal transplant from ___.

COMPARISON:  Renal transplant biopsy, ___ and renal transplant
ultrasound ___.

FINDINGS:  The transplant kidney is again seen in the right lower quadrant and
measures 12.3 cm.  A mild amount of perinephric fluid is noted.  No
hydronephrosis is seen.  The renal pelvis and proximal ureter are noted to be
echogenic in appearance, which could suggest a fungal UTI with urothelial
thickening or possibly redundant urothelium secondary to chronic dilatation as
a result of distention of the bladder.  No focal abnormality is seen in the
transplant kidney.  The bladder is only minimally distended and demonstrates
mild wall thickening.

DOPPLER EXAMINATION:  Color Doppler and pulse-wave Doppler images were
obtained.  Appropriate arterial waveforms with sharp upstrokes are seen in the
main renal artery.  Appropriate venous flow is seen in the main renal vein. 
Resistive range from 75 to 78.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Trace of perinephric fluid in the right lower quadrant.  No
hydronephrosis.  Thickening of the renal pelvis and proximal ureter could
represent redundant urothelium based on frequent distention of the bladder or
could represent a fungal UTI with urothelial thickening.  Clinical correlation
for fungal UTI is suggested.
2.  Mild thickening of the bladder wall is noted.
3.  Patent transplant kidney vasculature.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Ms. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , one of your hospital doctors. You're here today because you were scheduled for a heart catheterization and echo, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve been having more trouble breathing lately, especially when I lie down. I need three pillows just to sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned some chest discomfort too, especially with activity or lying flat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it feels like a squeezing, lasts a minute or so. It goes away when I sit up. I also feel very tired walking short distances.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We also noticed some swelling in your legs and your neck veins are a bit raised, which suggests fluid buildup. We’ll check your kidney function today since it’s important before doing the cath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My kidneys have been bad for years. I’ve had two transplants. I’m trying to avoid dialysis again. Is that going to be a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might be. Your baseline creatinine is around 3.0, but today it’s 3.9, which means your kidney function has worsened. That makes the cath riskier because the dye can hurt the kidneys more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So does that mean I can’t have the test? I’m worried about my heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discussing it with your cardiologist and nephrologist. Right now, the concern is that the cath could push you into needing dialysis. We don’t want that if you’re not ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want dialysis. Not now. Is there another way to check my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We may be able to do a stress test or imaging without dye later, but for now, we’re holding off on the cath. We’ll focus on managing your symptoms and protecting your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. But what about my chest pain? I don’t want to have a heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping you on aspirin and will increase your blood pressure meds to help your heart work easier. We’ll also give you nitroglycerin tablets to use if you have chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nitroglycerin? How do I use that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you have chest pain, you put one tablet under your tongue. If it doesn’t go away in 5 minutes, you can take another. Up to three. If it’s still there, call your cardiologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my blood pressure meds—are they changing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re increasing your carvedilol and amlodipine. But we stopped your lisinopril because it can affect your kidneys when they’re already stressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I’ve been on that for years. Is it safe to stop?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, in this case, it’s better to protect your kidneys. We’re monitoring everything closely. Your blood pressure is a bit high today, so the other meds will help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. I wanted to update you. Your chest X-ray shows no fluid in the lungs, which is good. But your kidney ultrasound shows some thickening in the bladder and ureter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that infection? Could that be making me feel worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be a fungal infection, but the urine culture only showed a few organisms, so it’s not a typical bacterial infection. We’ll watch it, but it’s not the main issue right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs this morning show your kidney function is a bit better—creatinine down to 3.4. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good! Does that mean I can have the heart test now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not quite. It’s improved, but still high risk. The team still thinks proceeding could lead to dialysis. We’re going to hold off and plan a follow-up with your cardiologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I just want to make sure my heart is okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And we do too. That’s why we’re increasing your heart meds and giving you the nitroglycerin. We’re also checking your tacrolimus level—it’s 4.4, which is in range, so your transplant is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed everything with cardiology and nephrology. The decision stands: no cath this time. But you’ll see Dr. ___ next week to discuss options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I trust you all. I just want to avoid dialysis as long as possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And we respect that. Your care plan is focused on your goals. We’ll keep managing your fluid overload and heart symptoms safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your labs are stable, and you’re feeling better. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do when I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue all your transplant meds—tacrolimus, sirolimus, prednisone. Keep taking the new doses of carvedilol and amlodipine. And use the nitroglycerin if you have chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no lisinopril?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct, we’re holding that for now to protect your kidneys. Your PCP, who is also your nephrologist, will manage that going forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have appointments set up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with your cardiologist and your nephrologist. They’ll help decide next steps for your heart and kidney evaluation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel better knowing we’re not rushing into something risky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to keep you safe and aligned with your wishes. You’re alert, walking fine, and your breathing is better. You can go home when the discharge papers are ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check—any chest pain last night or this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, none. I’ve been feeling pretty good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re cleared to go home. Take care, and follow up as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call if you have chest pain that doesn’t go away, or if you feel much more short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old female with a history of coronary artery disease, mitral regurgitation, and prior kidney and pancreas transplants was admitted for scheduled heart catheterization and transesophageal echocardiogram. She reported progressive shortness of breath, orthopnea, and exertional chest discomfort. Admission labs showed acute kidney injury with creatinine rising from a baseline of 2.6–3.2 to 3.9, prompting cancellation of the catheterization due to high risk of requiring dialysis. Her lisinopril was stopped, and carvedilol and amlodipine were increased to manage hypertension and cardiac workload. She was prescribed sublingual nitroglycerin for chest pain. Kidney ultrasound showed no acute obstruction but suggested possible urothelial thickening, though urine culture was not diagnostic. Her transplant function remained stable. She was discharged home after three days with follow-up arranged with cardiology and nephrology, with a focus on outpatient evaluation and respecting her preference to avoid dialysis.
